stem: An adult's spouse died 14 months ago. The client reports persistent intense longing, preoccupation with the death, and major impairment in daily functioning. Which condition should the nurse recognize as requiring further evaluation?
rationale: The American Psychiatric Association states that prolonged grief disorder in adults requires the death of a close person to have occurred at least 12 months earlier and may involve intense longing and/or preoccupation with the deceased together with significant distress or impairment. The client's 14-month timeline and disabling persistent grief pattern therefore warrant evaluation for prolonged grief disorder. B is correct as the condition to evaluate, but the vignette alone does not establish the full DSM-5-TR diagnosis: additional required symptoms, frequency/duration details, differential diagnosis, and whether the grief exceeds expected social, cultural, or religious norms must still be assessed. A underestimates the disabling persistent pattern, while C and D do not fit the described bereavement syndrome.
educational_objective: Recognize persistent disabling grief at least 12 months after the death of a close person as a pattern that warrants evaluation for prolonged grief disorder while avoiding diagnosis without the full DSM-5-TR criteria and cultural context.
source_version_date: APA patient/family page physician-reviewed August 2025; DSM-5-TR published 2022 and current in 2026
source_locator: Prolonged Grief Disorder > Symptoms and Diagnosis: intense longing and/or preoccupation; significant distress/problems in daily functioning; for adults the death must have occurred at least one year earlier; diagnosis additionally requires at least 3 listed symptoms nearly every day for at least the last month and grief lasting longer than expected by social, cultural, or religious norms. About DSM-5-TR confirms PGD is an included diagnosis and criteria require trained clinical judgment.
source_claim_supported: An adult with persistent intense longing/preoccupation and major functional impairment 14 months after a spouse's death should be evaluated for prolonged grief disorder, although the full DSM-5-TR criteria and cultural context must be assessed before diagnosis.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: recognize mental-health and coping alterations, assess grief/loss responses, provide psychosocial support, and identify findings requiring further mental-health evaluation.
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — prolonged grief and bereavement assessment

source_original.stem: An adult's spouse died 14 months ago. The client has persistent intense longing, preoccupation with the death, and major impairment in daily functioning. Which condition should be evaluated?
source_original.rationale: For adults, prolonged grief disorder is considered when a close person's death occurred at least 12 months earlier and persistent longing or preoccupation is associated with significant distress or functional impairment. Option B is the condition to evaluate; the full DSM-5-TR criteria and cultural context must still be assessed. The other choices do not fit this persistent bereavement pattern.
source_original.source_detail: Symptoms and Diagnosis: persistent intense longing and/or preoccupation with the deceased with significant distress or functional impairment; for adults the death must have occurred at least one year earlier, and diagnosis requires the full DSM-5-TR criteria with cultural context considered. APA page physician-reviewed August 2025; DSM-5-TR (2022) remains current and includes prolonged grief disorder; live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Psychosocial Integrity: mental-health symptom recognition, therapeutic communication, professional boundaries, coping and psychosocial support as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the prolonged-grief construct and key B, but explicitly framed the item as recognition for further evaluation rather than diagnosis because the stem does not contain every DSM-5-TR criterion. Strengthened the rationale with the additional symptom/frequency/cultural-context requirements and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current APA PGD guidance and DSM-5-TR; official NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: APA page physician-reviewed 2025-08; DSM-5-TR remains the current DSM text revision in 2026; live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: APA Prolonged Grief Disorder > Symptoms and Diagnosis; About DSM-5-TR > diagnostic criteria sets
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item does not diagnose PGD from incomplete data. It identifies a source-supported pattern warranting further evaluation and explicitly preserves the full criteria and cultural-context requirements.

distractor_audit.A: The persistent intense and functionally impairing pattern 14 months after loss warrants evaluation beyond assuming uncomplicated grief only.
distractor_audit.B: Correct condition to evaluate given the timeline and hallmark symptoms.
distractor_audit.C: Acute stress disorder does not fit this 14-month persistent bereavement presentation.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B matches the bereavement-specific timeline plus longing/preoccupation/functional impairment while remaining framed as evaluation rather than definitive diagnosis.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are diagnostic/clinical interpretations; the key is not established by a single isolated symptom alone.
audit_findings.blueprint: Psychosocial Integrity — grief/loss response and mental-health symptom recognition.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current APA PGD page, DSM-5-TR status, full-criteria caveat, all alternatives, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity and cueing. B remained uniquely best as a condition to evaluate.
